summary: An excerpt from the fiction book 'Book 10 — part 38' in which a venture capitalist visits an artist in Pico Rivera who makes sculptures from discarded electronics and scratched phone parts. He admires her work, which evokes his childhood longings for such objects. She says her business is not limited by scale, and she sells only through in-person commissions.
one_line: A venture capitalist visits an artist in Pico Rivera who makes sculptures from discarded electronics, and they argue over whether her craft can scale.
key_facts: A sculpture's eyes bear HP and Playstation logos, and its lips are made from inner-tube strips that carry the smallest recognizable logomarks.
The artist says the device works like an old-time phone and can look up old-style exchange numbers to try to connect a voice call.
The artist says most buyers want the device for its object-ness rather than its phone function.
The narrator describes the scratches on the sculptures as stories, each a memento mori for a long-dead instant in a stranger's life.
One sculpture is made from several generations of iPhones, with screens carved into abstract shapes and painted with networked OLEDs stitched into a single display.
The narrator says the iPhone sculpture gives the sense of holding a vampire, something transgressive, savage and dangerous.
The artist tosses the vampire sculpture high so it lands on its armored back, and says of it, 'You can't break it, it's made of garbage.'
The VC says he wanted these objects badly as a child, when each one seemed impossibly wonderful and out of reach.
The artist says these objects went from fetish items to six-for-a-buck in blister packs at the pharmacy checkout.
The artist says she mostly takes commissions, only from people who come down in person, and she will not sell online.
The artist says getting off email was the best gift she ever gave herself.
The artist invites visitors to come to Pico Rivera, where there is parking.
The VC says the artist cannot scale this business up, even with all the money in the world.
The artist replies that her business decomposes into four elements, materials acquisition, design, fabrication and retail, and that all four scale like crazy.
